Unconjugated bilirubin is too big to pass through membranes into bile ducts. It is converted into conjugated bilirubin by the enzyme Bilirubin-conjugating enzyme (BCE) in the liver. Conjugated bilirubin is then able to pass through the membranes of the bile ducts.  Haem is broken down into biliverden by heme-oxygenase. Biliverden is then converted into bilirubin by biliverden reductase.  Bilirubin is then converted into urobilinogen by the enzyme bilirubin reductase in the liver and kidney. Urobilinogen is then oxidised by intestinal bacteria to form a compound called beta-carotene. This compound is then oxidised to form urobilin which turns yellow. This yellow compound is then oxidised to form Stercobilin which gives faeces its brown colour. Green vegetables can also give faeces its green colour.

DPP-4 inhibitors stop the breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP, therefore they increase the amount of these incretins present in the body. Sulphonylureas increase the release of insulin from the beta cells of the pancreas. They do this by blocking K+ pumps in the cell membrane, causing depolarisation and therefore a greater influx of Ca2+ which causes the opening of more voltage gated channels for insulin.  Thiazolidinediones increase the sensitivity of cells to insulin, as well as stimulate insulin release from the beta cells of the pancreas. They do this by activating PPAR-gamma.  Alpha glucosidase inhibitors stop the breakdown of disaccharides to glucose and fructose in the gut, therefore they increase the time it takes for glucose to enter the bloodstream.  Incretin mimetics are dummy versions of GLP-1 which act on the beta cells of the pancreas to increase the release of insulin.

The correct answer is D. This statement is describing the changes that occur in the foetal heart when the baby is born that leads to the closure of the foramen ovale. The changes that occur are:1. The lungs are filled with air for the first time. This leads to the opening of the bronchi and the initiation of pulmonary blood flow. The left atrial pressure rises due to increased pulmonary venous return.2. The first breath is taken. This leads to a sudden drop in pressure in the pulmonary system. The alveoli are now well oxygenated and the arterioles dilate. This leads to increased blood flow into the left side of the heart.3. The increased left atrial pressure and decreased right atrial pressure leads to the closure of the foramen ovale. The pressure in the left atrium is now higher than the right. The foramen ovale is sealed and the oval fossa is formed. This becomes a bicuspid valve in adults.
